title: Jesus Heals the Man Born Blind

verses.text: Now as Jesus was passing by, He saw a man blind from birth,
and His disciples asked Him, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?"
Jesus answered, "Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him.
While it is daytime, we must do the works of Him who sent Me. Night is coming, when no one can work.
While I am in the world, I am the light of the world."
When Jesus had said this, He spit on the ground, made some mud, and applied it to the man's eyes.
Then He told him, "Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam" (which means "Sent"). So the man went and washed, and came back seeing.
At this, his neighbors and those who had formerly seen him begging began to ask, "Isn't this the man who used to sit and beg?"
Some claimed that he was, but others said, "No, he just looks like him." But the man kept saying, "I am the one."
"How then were your eyes opened?" they asked.
He answered, "The man they call Jesus made some mud and anointed my eyes, and He told me to go to Siloam and wash. So I went and washed and received my sight."
"Where is He?" they asked. "I do not know," he answered.
They brought to the Pharisees the man who had been blind.
Now the day on which Jesus had made the mud and opened his eyes was a Sabbath.
So the Pharisees also asked him how he had received his sight. The man answered, "He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and now I can see."

Because of this, some of the Pharisees said, "This man is not from God, for He does not keep the Sabbath." But others said, "How can a sinful man perform such signs?" And there was division among them.
So once again they asked the man who had been blind, "What do you say about Him, since it was your eyes He opened?" "He is a prophet," the man replied.
The Jews still did not believe that the man had been blind and had received his sight until they summoned his parents
and asked, "Is this your son, the one you say was born blind? So how is it that he can now see?"
His parents answered, "We know he is our son, and we know he was born blind.
But how he can now see or who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him. He is old enough to speak for himself."
His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jews. For the Jews had already determined that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue.
That was why his parents said, "He is old enough. Ask him."
So a second time they called for the man who had been blind and said, "Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner."
He answered, "Whether He is a sinner I do not know. There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!"
"What did He do to you?" they asked. "How did He open your eyes?"
He replied, "I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become His disciples?"
Then they heaped insults on him and said, "You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses.
We know that God spoke to Moses, but we do not know where this man is from."
"That is remarkable indeed!" the man said. "You do not know where He is from, and yet He opened my eyes.
We know that God does not listen to sinners, but He does listen to the one who worships Him and does His will.
Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind.
If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing."
They replied, "You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?" And they threw him out.
When Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, He found the man and said, "Do you believe in the Son of Man?"
"Who is He, Sir?" he replied. "Tell me so that I may believe in Him."
"You have already seen Him," Jesus answered. "He is the One speaking with you."
"Lord, I believe," he said. And he worshiped Jesus.
Then Jesus declared, "For judgment I have come into this world, so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind."
Some of the Pharisees who were with Him heard this, and they asked Him, "Are we blind too?"
"If you were blind," Jesus replied, "you would not be guilty of sin. But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains."

context.author: Traditionally the apostle John
context.genre: Theological narrative — the fifth of John's seven signs, told as an extended drama with a clear narrative arc as one man's testimony grows bolder under mounting pressure
context.audience: A broad, likely mixed Jewish and Gentile readership toward the end of the first century
context.setting: Archaeologists uncovered the actual first-century Pool of Siloam in 2004, at the southern end of Hezekiah's ancient water tunnel — pilgrims used its water in temple festival ceremonies, giving Jesus' instruction real, immediate significance beyond just a place to wash.
context.custom: Rabbinic tradition had expanded the Sabbath's prohibited categories of "work" to thirty-nine specific activities, including kneading — which is exactly what mixing spit and dirt into mud amounted to, giving the Pharisees their technical objection. By this point the Jewish authorities had already decided that confessing Jesus as the Christ meant expulsion from the synagogue — a real, serious social and economic penalty, not an empty threat, which explains the parents' careful evasiveness.
context.timelineImmediate: This single healing triggers an escalating five-stage interrogation — neighbors, then Pharisees twice, then the man's own parents — with the healed man's own testimony growing steadily bolder and more confident at each stage, ending in his expulsion and a direct, personal encounter with Jesus.
context.timelineBible: The disciples' opening question about whose sin caused the blindness reflects a common assumption Job's own friends made centuries earlier; Jesus' answer breaks that assumed link entirely, while His self-application as "light of the world" directly continues the claim He made just one chapter earlier at the Feast of Tabernacles.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus heals a man blind from birth, deliberately breaking the assumption that his condition must trace back to someone's sin. What follows is a five-round interrogation that only sharpens the man's own testimony each time it's challenged, climaxing in his simple, unshakeable line: "I was blind, but now I see." Expelled from the synagogue for his honesty, he's found again by Jesus Himself, and the chapter closes with Jesus naming the real inversion at play: the ones who claim to see are the ones who are truly blind.

translation.greek: Σιλωάμ, ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται Ἀπεσταλμένος (Silōam, ho hermēneuetai Apestalmenos)
translation.meaning: John pauses to translate the pool's name directly for the reader — "Siloam" means "Sent," a quiet but deliberate echo of Jesus' own repeated description of Himself throughout this Gospel as the One sent by the Father.

translation.english: I was blind, but now I see
translation.greek: τυφλὸς ὢν ἄρτι βλέπω (typhlos ōn arti blepō)
translation.meaning: The man's simplest and most famous line — he refuses to be drawn into theological argument about Jesus' status, sticking instead to the one fact he can testify to firsthand.
Used throughout this chapter in a deliberate double sense — literal physical blindness for the healed man, and a spiritual blindness Jesus applies pointedly to the Pharisees who claim to see clearly.

otBackground.note: Job's own suffering, wrongly assumed by his friends to trace back to personal sin — the same faulty assumption behind the disciples' opening question here.
The Servant of the Lord given "as a light... to open the eyes that are blind" — directly fulfilled in this sign.
Seeing without perceiving, hearing without understanding — the exact pattern Jesus names in the Pharisees at the chapter's close.

commentary.note: Henry calls out the disciples' question as 'uncharitably censorious' — assuming without evidence that this man must have committed some extraordinary sin to deserve such a fate. Jesus' answer, he notes, overturns two common assumptions at once: that such calamities are always direct punishment, and that they serve no larger purpose — here, the man's blindness becomes the very occasion for God's work to be seen.

Henry frames the healed beggar as an unlikely but effective witness: 'it is an encouragement to those who are concerned for the cause of Christ to hope that it shall never be lost for want of witnesses,' when even a poor blind beggar can be found standing firm against the very people most determined to discredit him.

Poole is precise about what Jesus' answer actually denies: not that suffering and sin are unrelated in general, but that this particular suffering was not brought about 'so as to bring this suffering upon him' by any specific wrongdoing of the man or his parents. The purpose instead lay in what God's power and goodness would go on to display through him.

overview.summary: Jesus heals a man born blind by anointing his eyes and sending him to wash in the pool of Siloam. The Pharisees question him and his parents, and the man worships Jesus while the leaders stay blind.
overview.settingLine: Jerusalem and the pool of Siloam.

history.t: Many assumed illness was punishment for sin, and Jesus rejected that.
People who confessed Jesus as Christ could be put out of the synagogue.

customs.t: Saliva was a folk remedy, though Jesus needed no medicine.
Water from Siloam was drawn each morning for the Tabernacles ceremony.

archaeology.t: A large stepped pool from the time of Jesus was uncovered in 2004.
The tunnel carries the Gihon spring water to Siloam.

overview.discussion: The man could say only, "I was blind, now I see." What simple thing can you say for certain?
overview.book: The fourth Gospel · 21 chapters. Written so readers would believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.
overview.author: John
